questions.prompt: A spherical ball is placed inside a cubic box. If the diameter of the ball equals the side of the box, what approximate percentage of the volume is empty?
hints: Let the cube side be a; the sphere radius is a/2.
Compute 100 times one minus the ratio of sphere volume to cube volume.
questions.solution: The cube volume is a³ and the sphere volume is (4π/3)(a/2)³=πa³/6. The empty fraction is 1−π/6≈0.4764, or 47.64%. The nearest listed percentage is 48%, option D.

similar_questions.solution: The circle area is πa²/4 and the square area is a². Empty percentage is 100(1−π/4)≈21.46%.

questions.prompt: All those who pass an entrance test take admission into a certain institute. Some graduate with a degree in 2 years, while some fail and are removed. All graduates get jobs in the same year. In 2022, no one took admission. Which does NOT follow necessarily?

options.D: No one got a job from the institute in 2024

hints: Distinguish passing a test from merely writing it.

questions.solution: Under the ordinary cohort reading (passing causes admission in that year and graduation takes exactly two years), no 2022 admission implies no 2022 passes, and no graduation of that cohort in 2024. Without an explicit year link for passing/admission, even B requires a temporal convention. No unique literal single answer is established.

questions.prompt: How many 4-digit numbers can be generated using digits 1,2,3,4,5 without repetition, with digit 1 always somewhere to the left of digit 2?
hints: The order condition requires both 1 and 2 to be included.
Choose the other two digits, then halve the permutations by exchanging 1 and 2.
questions.solution: Choose two additional digits from {3,4,5}: binomial(3,2)=3 choices. For each set of four distinct digits there are 4!=24 arrangements. Exchanging 1 and 2 pairs those with 1 left of 2 with those with 2 left of 1, so exactly 12 arrangements are valid. Total=3×12=36, option B.
questions.theory: Counting with restrictions begins by specifying exactly which objects must be present, whether repetition is allowed, and whether order matters. A permutation of k distinct selected objects has k! arrangements; choosing k objects from n gives binomial(n,k)=n!/[k!(n−k)!]. Multiplying these counts is legitimate when every choice admits the same number of arrangements. A symmetry exchanging two specified labels pairs arrangements in which the first label occurs earlier with arrangements in which the second occurs earlier. When both labels are required and distinct, precisely half the permutations satisfy the specified relative order. This argument cannot be applied blindly when one of the labels may be absent. Common pitfalls are counting combinations instead of ordered numbers, allowing forbidden repetitions, and overlooking a required label or a leading-zero restriction.

similar_questions.prompt: How many 3-digit numbers from 1,2,3,4 without repetition contain 1 and 2, with 1 before 2?
similar_questions.solution: Choose the third digit from {3,4}, giving 2 choices. Each triple has 3!/2=3 acceptable permutations. Total=2×3=6.

similar_questions.prompt: How many permutations of 1,2,3,4,5 place 1 before 2 before 3?
similar_questions.solution: All 5!=120 permutations split equally among the 3!=6 relative orders of 1,2,3. Exactly 120/6=20 satisfy the specified order.

questions.prompt: Which source Venn diagram is NOT consistent with: all A are B; no D is A; some A are C?

options.A: Diagram 1: C lies inside A, A inside B, D inside B disjoint from A
options.B: Diagram 2: A and C overlap inside B; D lies in C disjoint from A
options.C: Diagram 3: A=B, C overlaps A=B, D is outside B
options.D: Diagram 4: A, C and D are pairwise disjoint inside B

hints: Test each diagram against A⊆B, A∩D=∅ and A∩C≠∅.
The existential statement requires an overlap between A and C.
questions.solution: Diagrams 1,2,3 all put A inside (or equal to) B, separate A from D, and give A and C a nonempty overlap. Diagram 4 separates A from C, so A∩C=∅, contradicting “some A are C.” Therefore D is the inconsistent diagram.
questions.theory: A set A is a subset of B if every element of A is also in B. In a Venn diagram this means the entire region for A lies inside the region for B; equality is permitted unless a proper subset is explicitly required. The statement 'no D is A' is A∩D=∅ and requires disjoint regions. The statement 'some A are C' means A∩C is nonempty and needs an overlapping region containing a witness. Existential statements cannot be established by merely placing two disjoint circles inside a common larger set. A diagram is consistent if there exists an assignment of elements satisfying all the statements. Check each condition separately; diagrams with coincident labels can represent equality, while circles touching at a boundary should not be confused with an overlap of populations.

similar_questions.prompt: All cats are mammals; some cats are black. Can cats and black things be disjoint circles?
similar_questions.solution: No. The first condition puts the cat circle inside mammals. The second requires at least one element in cats∩black, so the cat and black regions must overlap.

similar_questions.prompt: If A=B and A∩C is nonempty, does this violate “all A are B”?
similar_questions.solution: No. Equality implies inclusion. For instance A=B={1,2} and C={2,3}; A⊆B and A∩C={2}.

questions.prompt: For integers n≥0, f_n:[−1,0]→ℝ is f_n(x)=x/(1−x)^n. Which statement is true about ∑_{n=0}^∞ f_n?

options.C: Absolutely convergent but not uniformly convergent
options.D: Uniformly convergent but not absolutely convergent

hints: For x<0 the summation is geometric; inspect x=0 separately.

questions.theory: A contour integral on the counterclockwise unit circle can be computed using z=e^(it), 0≤t≤2π, with dz=ie^(it)dt. On that circle the complex conjugate satisfies z̄=1/z. Consequently (1/2πi)∮zᵏdz equals one when k=−1 and zero for every other integer k. This is coefficient extraction for Laurent series and is also the residue theorem for monomials. The differential contributes an extra factor z under parametrization, so forgetting it shifts the exponent condition by one. The residue theorem applies to a positively oriented closed contour enclosing isolated singularities; reversing orientation changes the sign. Common pitfalls include substituting z̄=z, treating a nonholomorphic integrand as globally holomorphic, and applying the unit-circle identity away from the circle.

similar_questions.prompt: Evaluate (1/(2πi))∮_{|z|=1}z²z̄³dz.

questions.prompt: D is the unit disc; f:D→ℂ is holomorphic, f(0)=0, and ψ=|f|² satisfies ψ_xx+ψ_yy=0. Which statement is FALSE?

options.A: f can extend to an entire function on ℂ
options.B: f has infinitely many zeros in D
options.D: exp(f) cannot take every complex value

hints: Compute Δ|f|² for a holomorphic f.
Harmonicity forces f′=0; use the value at zero.
questions.solution: For holomorphic f, Δ|f|²=4|f′|². The given Laplacian is zero, so f′=0 throughout the connected disc and f is constant. Since f(0)=0, f≡0. It extends as the zero entire function, has every point of D as a zero, and exp(f)≡1 does not take all complex values. The zero function is a polynomial. Thus “f is not a polynomial,” option C, is false.
questions.theory: For a holomorphic function f=u+iv, both u and v are harmonic: their Laplacians u_xx+u_yy and v_xx+v_yy vanish. However the modulus squared |f|²=u²+v² is generally not harmonic. Differentiation using the Cauchy–Riemann equations gives Δ|f|²=4|f′|². Therefore harmonicity of |f|² on a connected domain forces f′=0 and f constant. If its value is zero at one point, it is identically zero. The zero function is a polynomial and extends to an entire function. The complex exponential never vanishes; if f≡0, exp(f)≡1. Common pitfalls include assuming the modulus of every holomorphic function is harmonic, excluding the zero polynomial, and confusing infinitely many zeros with a nonzero function that violates the identity theorem.

similar_questions.prompt: For f(z)=z, compute Δ|f|².
similar_questions.solution: |f|²=x²+y², whose Laplacian is 2+2=4. Since f′=1, the identity 4|f′|² also gives 4; the modulus squared is not harmonic.

similar_questions.prompt: If |f|² is harmonic on a connected domain and f(z₀)=3i, determine f.
similar_questions.solution: The identity implies f′=0, so f is constant. The given value determines f≡3i; then |f|²≡9 is harmonic.

questions.prompt: G(n) is the number of isomorphism classes of groups of order n>1. Which statement is true?

options.A: If G(n)=1, then n is prime

hints: Composite cyclic numbers can have a unique group.
For the gcd obstruction, separate nonsquarefree and squarefree n.
questions.solution: A is false: n=15 has gcd(15,φ(15))=gcd(15,8)=1, so all groups of order 15 are cyclic and G(15)=1. B is false: order 8 has C₈,C₄×C₂,C₂³,D₈,Q₈, five groups. To prove C, if p²|n, the abelian groups C_n and C_p×C_(n/p) are nonisomorphic. If n is squarefree and gcd(n,φ(n))>1, some p|n divides q−1 for a distinct prime q|n. A nontrivial homomorphism C_p→Aut(C_q) gives a nonabelian semidirect product of order pq; taking its direct product with C_(n/(pq)) gives a nonabelian order-n group distinct from C_n. Finally G(2^k) is at least the number of partitions of k, by abelian-group classification, and is unbounded. Therefore D fails and C is correct.
questions.theory: A finite group of prime order is cyclic by Lagrange's theorem: a nonidentity element generates a subgroup whose order must be the prime. Composite orders can also admit a unique group up to isomorphism. A positive integer n is a cyclic number precisely when gcd(n,φ(n))=1, where φ is Euler's totient; equivalently every group of order n is cyclic exactly under this condition. The obstruction is constructive: if p² divides n, two nonisomorphic abelian groups of order n can be formed; if n is squarefree and p divides q−1 for primes p,q dividing n, a nonabelian semidirect product of order pq exists. Group counts grow without bound along prime powers because distinct partitions give distinct finite abelian groups. Common pitfalls include extending the prime-order theorem to an “only if” statement and counting only abelian groups.

similar_questions.prompt: List groups of order 4 up to isomorphism.
similar_questions.solution: Either an element has order 4, yielding C₄, or every nonidentity element has order 2, yielding C₂×C₂. These are nonisomorphic because only C₄ has an element of order 4; G(4)=2.

similar_questions.prompt: Construct two nonisomorphic groups of order 21.
similar_questions.solution: C₂₁ is abelian. Since 3 divides 7−1, multiplication by 2 mod 7 has order 3 and defines C₇⋊C₃, with presentation a⁷=b³=1, bab⁻¹=a². It is nonabelian and has 21 elements, so it is not isomorphic to C₂₁.

questions.prompt: G has property (A) if every nontrivial homomorphism from G to any group is injective. Which group has (A)?
hints: A noninjective homomorphism has a nontrivial kernel.
The property is equivalent to having no proper nontrivial normal subgroup.
questions.solution: A nontrivial homomorphism has a proper kernel; if G is simple that kernel must be {e}, giving injectivity. Conversely, a proper nontrivial normal N produces the nontrivial noninjective map G→G/N. A₅ is simple, hence C satisfies the property. C₆ maps noninjectively onto C₂; S₅ maps onto {±1} by sign; the order-10 dihedral group maps onto C₂ with its order-5 rotations as kernel. These reject A,B,D.
questions.theory: A group homomorphism preserves multiplication, and its kernel is always a normal subgroup. The first isomorphism theorem identifies the image with the quotient by the kernel. Thus a homomorphism is injective exactly when its kernel is trivial. A nontrivial group is simple when its only normal subgroups are the identity subgroup and the whole group; this is precisely the condition that every nontrivial homomorphism out of it be injective. A proper nontrivial normal subgroup creates a nontrivial, noninjective quotient map. The alternating group A₅ is the smallest nonabelian simple group. The symmetric group S₅ has A₅ as a normal subgroup of index two, detected by the sign homomorphism. Dihedral groups have normal rotation subgroups. Common pitfalls include confusing simple with cyclic and testing only homomorphisms into the same group.

similar_questions.prompt: Does C₇ have the property?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Its only subgroups, hence its only normal subgroups, are {e} and C₇ by Lagrange. Any nontrivial homomorphism has trivial kernel and is injective.

similar_questions.prompt: Does C₄ have the property?
similar_questions.solution: No. Reduction modulo 2 is a surjective homomorphism C₄→C₂. Its kernel {0,2} is nontrivial, so the map is noninjective while its image is nontrivial.

questions.prompt: For which ideal I in ℂ[x,y] is ℂ[x,y]/I NOT an integral domain?
hints: Factor x²+y² over the stated field ℂ.
For the other options, identify the quotient as a familiar field or domain.
questions.solution: For C, x²+y²=(x+iy)(x−iy). Neither linear factor belongs to the ideal generated by the degree-two polynomial, so their nonzero residue classes multiply to zero. Thus this quotient is not a domain. For A the quotient is ℂ; for B substituting y=−x gives ℂ[x]; for D the relation xy=1 identifies the quotient with the Laurent polynomial domain ℂ[x,x⁻¹]. Hence C is correct.
questions.theory: An integral domain is a nonzero commutative ring with identity and no zero divisors. For a commutative ring R and proper ideal I, the quotient R/I is an integral domain if and only if I is prime. A maximal ideal yields a field and is therefore prime. To disprove primality, find factors not belonging to I whose product belongs to I. In a polynomial ring over a field, a principal ideal generated by an irreducible polynomial is prime because the ring is a unique factorization domain. Factorization depends on the coefficient field: x²+y² splits over ℂ as (x+iy)(x−iy). Quotient substitutions such as y=−x or y=x⁻¹ often identify a domain directly. Common pitfalls include using real irreducibility over complex coefficients and mistaking a reducible polynomial for a maximal ideal.

similar_questions.prompt: Is ℂ[x]/(x²+1) an integral domain?
similar_questions.solution: No. x²+1=(x−i)(x+i). Both linear factors have nonzero residue classes but their product vanishes. The quotient has zero divisors.

similar_questions.prompt: Identify ℝ[x,y]/(y−x²).
similar_questions.solution: Substitution y=x² defines a surjective map to ℝ[x] with kernel (y−x²), so the quotient is ℝ[x], an integral domain.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true?

options.A: {m+n exp(2πi/3) | m,n∈ℤ} is dense in ℂ
options.B: Open connected subsets of ℝ³ need not be path connected
options.C: If p:X→ℝ is continuous, surjective and open, with every fiber connected, then X is connected
options.D: Compact subsets of any infinite topological space are closed

hints: For C, suppose X has a separation into two open sets.
Connected fibers cannot meet both sides; openness then separates ℝ.
questions.solution: A is false: the imaginary parts are n√3/2, a discrete set, leaving open discs with no points. B is false because open Euclidean sets are locally path connected, so connectedness implies path connectedness. For C, suppose X=U∪V is a separation. Each connected fiber lies wholly in U or V, so p(U) and p(V) are disjoint nonempty sets covering ℝ; since p is open, they form a separation of ℝ, impossible. D is false in an infinite indiscrete space: a nonempty proper singleton is compact but not closed. Thus C alone is true.
questions.theory: A topological space is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open subsets. Path connectedness requires a continuous path between every pair of points and implies connectedness; the converse fails in general. Open subsets of Euclidean space are locally path connected, so an open connected subset is path connected. Continuous images of connected spaces are connected. For a continuous open surjection with connected fibers, a separation of the domain would induce a separation of the range: each fiber must lie wholly in one side. Compact subsets are closed in Hausdorff spaces, not in arbitrary spaces. A lattice generated by two real-linearly independent complex numbers is discrete rather than dense. Common pitfalls include omitting Hausdorff hypotheses and transferring Euclidean path properties to all topological spaces.

similar_questions.prompt: Why is a compact subset of a Hausdorff space closed?
similar_questions.solution: For a point outside the compact set, Hausdorffness separates it from each point of the set. A finite subcover of the set yields finitely many separating neighborhoods; their intersection is an open neighborhood of the external point avoiding the compact set. The complement is open.

similar_questions.prompt: If p:X→Y is an open surjection with connected fibers and Y connected, is X connected?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. A separation U,V would force each fiber into one side, making the nonempty disjoint open images p(U),p(V) a separation of Y. This contradicts connectedness.

questions.theory: For a second-order linear equation y″+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=0, changing the independent variable s=s(x) requires s′≠0 and the chain rule y′=s′Y_s, y″=(s′)²Y_ss+s″Y_s. questions.prompt: xu_x+yu_y=u for (x,y)≠(0,0), with u(x,1)=√(1+x²) for x∈ℝ. Which statement is true?
hints: Characteristics are rays through the origin.
Which rays intersect the data line y=1?
questions.solution: Characteristics obey (x,y,u)=eˢ(a,1,√(1+a²)), giving u=√(x²+y²) for y>0. This implies by continuity u(1,0)=1, disproving A. C fails already at y=2, and D fails at (0,1) versus (1/2,1/2), both above the axis. B is the intended radial answer, but the data do not meet lower-half-plane rays and therefore do not force radial symmetry there. Let r=√(x²+y²) and y_−=max(−y,0). The C² function u=r+y_−³/r² on the punctured plane is positively homogeneous of degree one, hence satisfies the PDE by Euler’s identity, and has the required data at y=1. Yet u(0,1)=1 and u(0,−1)=2, although radii coincide, disproving B. Thus none of the globally quantified options follows literally. On the characteristic-covered domain y>0, or with an added requirement u=r globally, B is correct.
questions.theory: The method of characteristics converts a first-order linear PDE a u_x+b u_y=c u into ordinary differential equations dx/ds=a, dy/ds=b, du/ds=c u. Initial data determine the solution only on characteristic curves meeting the initial curve, and local uniqueness requires a noncharacteristic initial curve. For xu_x+yu_y=u, characteristics are rays and u is positively homogeneous of degree one; data on y=1 determine only rays in the upper half-plane. For the one-dimensional wave equation u_tt−u_xx=0, the general twice differentiable solution is F(x+t)+G(x−t). A condition at x=0 relates F and G only at the corresponding arguments, creating identities inside the relevant characteristic cone. Common pitfalls include claiming global uniqueness outside the domain reached by the data and replacing homogeneity by radial symmetry without justification.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve xu_x+yu_y=u with u(x,1)=x on y>0.
similar_questions.solution: Characteristics have a=x/y and scale y. Therefore u(x,y)=y·a=x. This satisfies both the PDE and the data; lower rays remain undetermined unless further data are supplied.

similar_questions.prompt: Show u(x,y)=r sin(3θ) is degree-one homogeneous.

questions.prompt: f:ℝ→ℝ has sup_{x≠y}|f(x)−f(y)|/|x−y|=L with 1<L<∞. A differentiable h has |h′|≤3/4. For α>0 set g=αf+h. Iteration x_(k+1)=g(x_k) converges to the fixed-point solution for every x₀ if:
hints: Bound the Lipschitz constant of g by the triangle inequality.
Banach’s theorem requires αL+3/4<1.
questions.solution: By the mean value theorem, |h(x)−h(y)|≤(3/4)|x−y|. Therefore |g(x)−g(y)|≤(αL+3/4)|x−y|. If α<1/(4L), this constant is below one, so Banach’s theorem on complete ℝ gives a unique fixed point and convergence from every start. The larger proposed bounds are not sufficient: choose f(x)=Lx and h(x)=3x/4 and select α satisfying the proposed bound but αL+3/4>1; then nonzero iterates diverge. Thus D is correct.
questions.theory: A map g on a metric space is a contraction if |g(x)−g(y)|≤q|x−y| for a fixed q<1. Banach's fixed-point theorem states that a contraction from a nonempty complete metric space into itself has one fixed point and every iteration x_(k+1)=g(x_k) converges to it. The real line with its usual distance is complete. A differentiable function with |h′|≤c is c-Lipschitz by the mean value theorem. Sums of Lipschitz maps satisfy the sum of their constants; multiplying by a scalar multiplies the constant by its absolute value. Thus g=αf+h has guaranteed constant at most αL+c. The bound must be strictly less than one. Common pitfalls include reversing an inequality for α and assuming mere continuity or a Lipschitz constant above one guarantees convergence.

similar_questions.prompt: For g(x)=x/2+1 find the fixed point and iterates.
similar_questions.solution: The fixed point solves x=x/2+1, giving x*=2. Subtracting 2 from the recurrence gives x_k−2=2⁻ᵏ(x₀−2), which tends to zero.

similar_questions.prompt: If f has Lipschitz constant 5 and |h′|≤1/2, what α guarantees contraction of αf+h?
similar_questions.solution: The constant is at most 5α+1/2. Requiring it below 1 gives α<1/10 for α≥0; then all real starting points converge uniquely.

questions.prompt: S is the set of all Euler–Lagrange solutions of minimizing ∫₀¹[y²+(y′)²]dx with y(0)=y(1)=0 and ∫₀¹y²dx=1. Find {φ(1/2):φ∈S}.
hints: Use a multiplier for the integral constraint to obtain a sine eigenvalue problem.
All stationary modes matter, including even modes that vanish at the midpoint.
questions.solution: For the augmented integrand (1−λ)y²+y′², Euler–Lagrange gives y″+(λ−1)y=0. The endpoints and nonzero normalization require λ−1=(kπ)² and y=±√2 sin(kπx), k≥1. At x=1/2, sin(kπ/2) is 0 for even k and ±1 for odd k. Thus the set is {−√2,0,√2}, D. Restricting to actual minimizers k=1 would give A, but S explicitly includes every Euler–Lagrange solution.
questions.theory: An isoperimetric variational problem minimizes an integral subject to endpoint conditions and an additional integral constraint. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier turns the problem into an unconstrained Euler–Lagrange equation for the augmented integrand. For ∫(y²+y′²) with ∫y²=1 and zero endpoints, the stationary functions solve a Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem and are normalized sine modes. Each mode satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations, but only the lowest-frequency mode minimizes the energy. Its higher-frequency companions are stationary points with larger objective values. Orthogonality and ∫₀¹sin²(kπx)dx=1/2 give the normalization √2. Common pitfalls include identifying every stationary solution as a minimizer, ignoring the integral constraint when choosing amplitude, and replacing the set of all stationary midpoint values with the midpoint values of the minimizers only.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the minimum value of the constrained functional.
similar_questions.solution: For the kth normalized sine, ∫y²=1 and ∫y′²=k²π². Thus J=1+k²π², minimized at k=1 with value 1+π².

similar_questions.prompt: For zero endpoints on [0,L], normalize the kth sine and find midpoint values.
similar_questions.solution: ∫₀ᴸsin²(kπx/L)dx=L/2, so y=±√(2/L)sin(kπx/L). At L/2 the values are 0 for even k and ±√(2/L) for odd k.

questions.prompt: Let λ∈ℝ and K:[0,1]²→ℝ be such that every solution of u″+λu=0, u′(0)=u(0),u′(1)=0 satisfies u(x)+λ∫₀¹K(x,t)u(t)dt=0. Then K is:
hints: The usual intended kernel inverts u″ under the two mixed boundary conditions.
But test whether the literal homogeneous-solution condition determines K when λ=0.
questions.solution: For the intended Green kernel G of d²/dx², take G=−1−x for x≤t and G=−1−t for t<x. It is continuous; its x derivative jumps from −1 to 0, giving jump 1. Also G_x(0,t)=G(0,t)=−1 and G_x(1,t)=0. Hence G solves the inverse problem and u=G(−λu), which gives the stated integral equation. This is option B. However the literal condition does not force a unique kernel: choose the allowed λ=0. The BVP u″=0 gives u=ax+b, a=b from the left condition and a=0 from the right, so u≡0. Every K then satisfies the stated integral equation, including all four options. Thus B is the conventional canonical Green-kernel answer, conditional on requiring K to represent the inverse differential operator (or the equivalence uniformly in λ); the source as written is underdetermined.
questions.theory: A Green kernel inverts a differential operator together with homogeneous boundary conditions. For L=d²/dx², the kernel is piecewise affine in x away from x=t, is continuous at t, and has derivative jump G_x(t+,t)−G_x(t−,t)=1. Its endpoint behavior must satisfy the same boundary conditions as the solution. Then u(x)=∫G(x,t)f(t)dt solves u″=f, and u″+λu=0 becomes u+λ∫G u=0. Sign conventions matter: the kernel for −d²/dx² is the negative of the kernel for d²/dx². However a condition tested only on solutions of one fixed homogeneous eigenvalue equation does not uniquely identify the kernel, especially when zero is the only solution. Common pitfalls include neglecting the derivative jump, confusing mixed and Dirichlet boundaries, and assuming uniqueness from a vacuous homogeneous test.

similar_questions.prompt: Find G for u″=f, u(0)=u(1)=0.
similar_questions.solution: Take G=x(t−1) for x≤t and t(x−1) for t<x. It vanishes at both endpoints, is continuous at x=t, and its derivative jump is t−(t−1)=1. Therefore u=∫Gf.

similar_questions.prompt: Why does a zero-only homogeneous BVP fail to determine a kernel?
similar_questions.solution: If u≡0 is the only solution, then u+λ∫Ku=0 reduces to 0=0 for every K. The condition imposes no restriction on any kernel value.

questions.source_note: B is the canonical mixed-boundary Green kernel, fully derived. As literally stated for arbitrary fixed λ, λ=0 gives only the zero solution and makes all kernels satisfy the condition, so uniqueness is not logically established.

questions.prompt: Two blocks of mass m are linked by a flexible inelastic cord of mass M and length l. One block is on a smooth table, the other hangs distance x below its edge. The cord potential is −Mgx²/(2l). Find ẍ.
hints: Include both blocks and the whole cord in the kinetic energy.
Differentiate the total gravitational potential with respect to x.
questions.solution: All moving pieces have speed ẋ, so T=(2m+M)ẋ²/2. The total potential is V=−mgx−Mgx²/(2l). Euler–Lagrange gives (2m+M)ẍ=mg+(Mg/l)x. Therefore ẍ=(g/l)(ml+Mx)/(2m+M), option D. A,B have incorrect dimensions and C omits one block from the inertia.
questions.theory: For a mechanical system with one generalized coordinate x, the Lagrangian is kinetic energy minus potential energy, L=T−V. Its Euler–Lagrange equation is d/dt(∂L/∂ẋ)−∂L/∂x=0. An inextensible cord makes both attached blocks and every cord element move with the same speed, so kinetic energy includes all moving masses. Taking the table edge as zero height, a hanging block contributes −mgx to potential energy, and a uniform hanging cord of density M/l contributes −Mgx²/(2l). The generalized gravitational force is −dV/dx. If the kinetic coefficient is constant, acceleration equals generalized force divided by total moving mass. Common pitfalls include omitting one block's inertia, treating only the hanging cord as moving, and accepting a formula whose units are not acceleration.

similar_questions.prompt: Set cord mass M=0 and find the acceleration.
similar_questions.solution: The force is mg and total moving mass is 2m, so ẍ=g/2. The general expression reduces to exactly this when M=0.

similar_questions.prompt: If M=m and x=l/2, find acceleration.
similar_questions.solution: Substitute into ẍ=(g/l)(ml+mx)/(3m). At x=l/2 the numerator is (3/2)ml, giving ẍ=g/2.

questions.prompt: Find lim_{n→∞}∫_[0,1]^n (x₁²+⋯+xₙ²)/(x₁+⋯+xₙ) dx₁⋯dxₙ.
hints: Interpret the integral as an expectation of independent uniform variables.
Apply the law of large numbers and bound the ratio by 1.
questions.solution: Let X_i be iid U(0,1). The integral is E[(∑X_i²)/(∑X_i)]. By the strong law, n⁻¹∑X_i²→1/3 and n⁻¹∑X_i→1/2 almost surely, so the ratio tends to 2/3. Because 0≤X_i²≤X_i, the ratio lies in [0,1] outside the all-zero event of probability zero. Dominated convergence therefore gives limit 2/3, option D.
questions.theory: Expectation is integration against a probability measure. For independent uniform coordinates on [0,1], an integral over the unit cube is the expectation of the same expression in independent U(0,1) variables. The strong law of large numbers states that sample averages of integrable independent identically distributed variables converge almost surely to their expectations. Ratios converge when the limiting denominator is nonzero. The dominated convergence theorem passes an almost-sure limit through expectation when all random variables are bounded in magnitude by one integrable bound. Bayes' theorem instead combines prior probabilities with conditional likelihoods and normalizes their products. Common pitfalls include dividing expectations instead of applying an asymptotic law, ignoring a zero-denominator point of measure zero, and failing to normalize posterior weights.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the limit of E[(∑X_i³)/(∑X_i)] for iid U(0,1).
similar_questions.solution: The two sample means tend to EX³=1/4 and EX=1/2. Their ratio tends to 1/2 and is bounded by 1, so dominated convergence gives 1/2.

similar_questions.prompt: For iid Bernoulli(p), p>0, find the limit of ∑X_i²/∑X_i.
similar_questions.solution: Since X_i²=X_i, the ratio is 1 whenever the denominator is positive. The denominator is eventually positive almost surely; hence the limit and limiting expectation are 1.

questions.prompt: Urn U_k contains 2k white and k² black balls, k=1,…,5. Choose U_k with probability proportional to k+2, then draw one ball. Given it is white, find P(U₅|white).

similar_questions.prompt: Choose two urns equally; their white fractions are 1/4 and 3/4. Given white, find probability of the second urn.
similar_questions.solution: Joint weights are (1/2)(1/4)=1/8 and (1/2)(3/4)=3/8. Normalize the second by their sum 1/2 to obtain 3/4.

similar_questions.prompt: Urn priors are proportional to 1,2,3 and white probabilities are 1,1/2,1/3. Find posterior priors given white.
similar_questions.solution: Each unnormalized weight is 1. Their sum is 3, so the posterior is uniform: each urn has probability 1/3.

questions.prompt: True/False answers satisfy P(next True|True)=3/4 and P(next False|False)=2/3. For 100 questions, approximate P(the 100th answer is True).
hints: Let p_n be the True probability and use total probability.
Solve the stationary equation; the finite-step correction decays geometrically.
questions.solution: P(next True|False)=1/3. Therefore p_(n+1)=(3/4)p_n+(1/3)(1−p_n)=1/3+(5/12)p_n. The stationary solution satisfies p*=1/3+(5/12)p*, giving p*=4/7. More exactly p₁₀₀=4/7+(5/12)⁹⁹(p₁−4/7); the correction is negligible for any initial probability. Thus B is the requested approximation.
questions.theory: For a two-state transition system, let p_n be the probability of state T at step n. If P(T next|T now)=a and P(T next|F now)=b, total probability gives p_(n+1)=a p_n+b(1−p_n)=b+(a−b)p_n. The stationary value is p*=b/(1−a+b), provided the denominator is nonzero. Subtraction gives p_n−p*=(a−b)^(n−1)(p_1−p*). When |a−b|<1, dependence on the initial distribution decays geometrically. Stationarity does not mean independence: consecutive states may remain correlated. In queueing systems with nonexponential service times, the number of customers alone is generally not Markov because the residual service distribution depends on age. Common pitfalls include using a stationary value as an exact finite-step probability and assuming the memoryless property for a gamma service distribution.

similar_questions.prompt: A two-state system has P(T|T)=0.8 and P(T|F)=0.2. Find its stationary True probability.
With P(T|T)=3/4 and P(T|F)=1/3, and p₁=1, compute p₂.
similar_questions.solution: p₂=3/4 directly. The formula gives 4/7+(5/12)(1−4/7)=4/7+5/28=3/4, confirming the recurrence.

questions.prompt: X~Binomial(9,θ), 0.7<θ<1, and Y~Poisson(λ), λ>0. If 3E(Y)=E(X), which is true?
hints: Use the mean relation to eliminate λ.
Divide the two variances and apply θ>0.7.
questions.solution: E(X)=9θ and E(Y)=λ, so λ=3θ. Var(X)=9θ(1−θ), Var(Y)=3θ. Their ratio is 3(1−θ), which lies strictly between 0 and 0.9. Thus Var(X)<Var(Y), D, and all the other intervals are excluded.
questions.theory: The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number n of independent Bernoulli trials with common probability p; its mean is np and variance np(1−p). A Poisson distribution of parameter λ has both mean and variance λ. A gamma distribution with shape α and scale β has density x^(α−1)e^(−x/β)/[Γ(α)β^α] for x>0. Its Laplace transform is E(e^(−sX))=(1+βs)^(−α). Ratios of variances can simplify after substituting a relation between means, and parameter inequalities then determine which interval contains the ratio. Common pitfalls include confusing gamma scale with rate, forgetting the binomial factor 1−p, and assuming equal means imply equal variances. Check strict inequalities carefully when parameters are specified in an open interval.

similar_questions.prompt: For X~Binomial(10,p), Y~Poisson(λ), E X=E Y, compare variances.
similar_questions.solution: λ=10p, so Var X/Var Y=1−p<1 for 0<p<1. Therefore binomial variance is smaller when the means coincide.

similar_questions.prompt: If 2E Y=E X and X~Binomial(n,p), find when Var X<Var Y.
similar_questions.solution: λ=np/2, so the variance ratio is 2(1−p). This is below 1 exactly when p>1/2.

questions.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ iid Gamma(shape α>0, scale 1), n≥2. Find the most powerful rejection region for H₀:α=1 versus H₁:α=2.
hints: Write both simple-hypothesis densities.
Cancel the common exponential factors in their likelihood ratio.
questions.solution: f₀(x)=e⁻ˣ and f₁(x)=xe⁻ˣ because Γ(1)=Γ(2)=1. For the sample, L₁/L₀=∏X_i. The Neyman–Pearson lemma rejects for large likelihood ratio, hence ∏X_i>C, A. C is chosen to attain the required size. The sums in B,D do not determine this ratio, and C selects its wrong tail.
questions.theory: The Neyman–Pearson lemma identifies a most powerful test of a simple null against a simple alternative: reject for large likelihood ratio f₁/f₀, randomizing at a threshold if needed to achieve the specified size. Size is the null rejection probability, while power is the alternative rejection probability. Reversing the hypotheses reverses the likelihood ratio, so complementing a most powerful test produces the appropriate low-ratio rejection region for the reverse test. Discrete test statistics can make exact target size impossible without randomization; the boundary rejection probability is found from a linear equation. Likelihood factors common to null and alternative cancel. Common pitfalls include confusing power with type-II error, choosing the tail by intuition rather than likelihood ratio, and overlooking randomization in a small sample.

similar_questions.prompt: For Gamma(shape 1,scale 1) versus Gamma(shape 3,scale 1), find the LR.
similar_questions.solution: Each density ratio is x²/Γ(3)=x²/2, so the sample ratio is 2⁻ⁿ(∏X_i)². It increases with the product, giving a large-product rejection region.

similar_questions.prompt: For iid exponential observations, test rate 1 versus rate 2.
similar_questions.solution: The sample likelihood ratio is 2ⁿe^(−∑X_i), which decreases with the sum. Most powerful rejection is for ∑X_i below a threshold.

questions.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ iid Uniform(θ,1−θ), n≥2, −∞<θ<1/2. Find the MLE of θ.
hints: Find the two upper bounds on θ imposed by the sample lying in its support.
Within the feasible region the likelihood increases as the interval shrinks.
questions.solution: Let m=min X_i and M=max X_i. The support requires θ≤m and M≤1−θ, equivalently θ≤1−M. On that feasible set L(θ)=(1−2θ)⁻ⁿ, a strictly increasing function of θ. Its maximum is at the largest feasible θ=min(m,1−M). Thus C is correct. The other formulas may violate one or both support conditions.
questions.theory: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses a parameter value maximizing the joint density of the observed sample as a function of that parameter. For uniform distributions with parameter-dependent endpoints, support inequalities are part of the likelihood and are often more important than differentiating the density. A Uniform(θ,1−θ) sample has likelihood (1−2θ)^(−n) when θ≤X_(1) and θ≤1−X_(n), and zero otherwise. Within the feasible parameter interval the likelihood increases with θ, so the largest admissible value is selected. Order statistics X_(1) and X_(n) summarize the support constraints. Under the usual closed-endpoint density convention the boundary maximum is attained; endpoint choices have probability zero under sampling. Common pitfalls include ignoring support restrictions, using a maximum instead of a minimum when both upper bounds must hold, and assuming θ must be positive.

similar_questions.prompt: For sample 0.2,0.3,0.7 from Uniform(θ,1−θ), find the MLE.
similar_questions.solution: m=0.2, M=0.7, so θ̂=min(0.2,0.3)=0.2. The resulting support [0.2,0.8] contains all observations and is the narrowest admissible symmetric interval.

similar_questions.prompt: For sample −2,0,1.5, find θ̂.
similar_questions.solution: m=−2 and 1−M=−0.5, so θ̂=−2. The allowed parameter may be negative; the fitted interval [−2,3] includes every observation.

questions.prompt: In Y_i=β₀+β₁x_i1+⋯+β_px_ip+ε_i, n>p+1, errors are uncorrelated with mean zero and common variance σ²>0. Let Ŷ be least-squares fits and ε̂_i=Y_i−Ŷ_i. Which statement is true?
hints: Use the orthogonal projection H onto the design column space.
Residual covariance is σ²(I−H), and 0≤h_ii≤1.
questions.solution: Ŷ=HY and ε̂=(I−H)Y=(I−H)ε. Since H is symmetric idempotent, Cov ε̂=σ²(I−H). Hence Var ε̂_i=σ²(1−h_ii)≤σ²=Var ε_i, proving A. Off-diagonal residual covariances are −σ²h_ik and generally nonzero, rejecting B. Var Ŷ_i=σ²h_ii generally differs from σ², rejecting C. Finally EŶ=HXβ=Xβ=EY, rejecting D.
questions.theory: In a linear regression model Y=Xβ+ε with Eε=0 and Cov ε=σ²I, least squares projects Y orthogonally onto the column space of the design matrix X. The hat matrix H is that orthogonal projection and satisfies H′=H and H²=H. Fitted values are HY and residuals are (I−H)Y. Their covariance matrices are σ²H and σ²(I−H), respectively. Each diagonal h_ii lies in [0,1], so residual variance is σ²(1−h_ii)≤σ². Residuals are generally correlated even when original errors are uncorrelated, since off-diagonal covariance is −σ²h_ik. Fitted values are unbiased for the model mean. Common pitfalls include treating residuals as original independent errors, confusing fitted variance with response variance, and assuming normality is needed for these covariance identities.

similar_questions.prompt: For an intercept-only model with n observations, find residual variances and covariances.
similar_questions.solution: H=(1/n)11′. Each residual variance is σ²(1−1/n), and for i≠j covariance is −σ²/n. Residuals are correlated even though the original errors are uncorrelated.

similar_questions.prompt: Show fitted values and residuals are uncorrelated.
similar_questions.solution: Their cross covariance is σ²H(I−H)=σ²(H−H²)=0. This holds without normality; normality would further imply independence.

questions.theory: A Wishart matrix W_p(ν,Σ) can be represented as the sum of ν outer products of independent mean-zero p-variate normal vectors with covariance Σ. For a partitioned Wishart matrix, the Schur complement of a leading block has a lower-dimensional Wishart distribution with degrees of freedom reduced by the size of that leading block and scale equal to the conditional covariance Schur complement. In dimension two, Z−Y²/X is the residual sum of squares from regressing the second normal coordinate on the first, using no intercept. Its distribution is (σ₂₂−σ₂₁²/σ₁₁)χ²_(ν−1). A chi-square variable with k degrees of freedom has mean k and variance 2k. Common pitfalls include retaining ν instead of ν−1 degrees of freedom, forgetting to square the scale when computing variance, and confusing a Wishart scale matrix with its mean.

questions.prompt: A population of N units has attribute proportion P. An SRS without replacement of size 2≤n<N has sample proportion p. Which is unbiased for P(1−P)?
hints: Use E[p(1−p)]=P(1−P)−Var p.
Insert the finite population correction, then invert the remaining factor.
questions.solution: Var p=[(N−n)/((N−1)n)]P(1−P). Thus E[p(1−p)]=[1−(N−n)/((N−1)n)]P(1−P)=[N(n−1)/((N−1)n)]P(1−P). Multiplying by (N−1)n/[N(n−1)] makes the estimator unbiased, giving D. C is the with-replacement correction and retains a finite-population bias here.
questions.theory: Simple random sampling without replacement gives every n-element subset of an N-element population equal probability. For a binary attribute with population proportion P, the sample proportion p is unbiased: Ep=P. Dependence among sampled units produces the finite population correction, Var(p)=P(1−P)(N−n)/[(N−1)n]. Consequently E[p(1−p)]=P(1−P)−Var(p), so the naive product p(1−p) is biased downward. An unbiased estimator of P(1−P) is obtained by dividing by the exact proportionality factor, not by merely applying the independent-sample factor n/(n−1). The correction approaches that independent factor as N grows. Common pitfalls include substituting a variance estimator for an estimator of the population product and mixing denominator conventions N and N−1 for finite-population variance.

similar_questions.prompt: For N=10,n=5, give the correction to p(1−p).
similar_questions.solution: The unbiased multiplier is (9·5)/(10·4)=9/8. Thus (9/8)p(1−p) is unbiased for P(1−P).

similar_questions.prompt: What happens if the full population is sampled, n=N?
similar_questions.solution: Then p=P exactly and no correction is needed. The multiplier (N−1)N/[N(N−1)] equals 1, agreeing with the census interpretation.

questions.prompt: An M/G/1 queue has arrival rate λ=1 and iid service density g(x)=xe⁻ˣ for x>0, zero otherwise. I_i=1 if the first transition from i is to i−1, and 0 if it is to i+1. Find Var(I₂).
hints: If observation starts when service starts, a departure wins exactly when S<A.
Use the gamma Laplace transform; inspect the service-age assumption.
questions.solution: Under the usual intended fresh-service convention, let S~Gamma(2,rate 1) and A~Exp(1) be independent. Then P(I₂=1)=P(S<A)=E(e⁻ˢ)=∫₀∞s e⁻²ˢds=1/4. A Bernoulli indicator has variance p(1−p), giving (1/4)(3/4)=3/16, C. Literally, an M/G/1 queue observed merely “from state 2” does not specify service age, and the customer count alone is not Markov. If current service has age a, its residual R has P(R>r|S>a)=e⁻ʳ(a+r+1)/(a+1); hence E(e⁻ᴿ)=(2a+1)/[4(a+1)]. At age 1, p=3/8 and Var=15/64, different from C. Therefore C requires the fresh-service interpretation; the literal state-only description is underdetermined.
questions.theory: For a two-state transition system, let p_n be the probability of state T at step n. If P(T next|T now)=a and P(T next|F now)=b, total probability gives p_(n+1)=a p_n+b(1−p_n)=b+(a−b)p_n. The stationary value is p*=b/(1−a+b), provided the denominator is nonzero. Subtraction gives p_n−p*=(a−b)^(n−1)(p_1−p*). When |a−b|<1, dependence on the initial distribution decays geometrically. Stationarity does not mean independence: consecutive states may remain correlated. In queueing systems with nonexponential service times, the number of customers alone is generally not Markov because the residual service distribution depends on age. Common pitfalls include using a stationary value as an exact finite-step probability and assuming the memoryless property for a gamma service distribution.

similar_questions.prompt: With fresh Gamma(3,rate 1) service and Exp(1) arrival, find the departure-first probability.
similar_questions.solution: The gamma Laplace transform gives E(e⁻ˢ)=(1+1)⁻³=1/8. The Bernoulli variance is (1/8)(7/8)=7/64.

similar_questions.prompt: With exponential service rate μ and Poisson arrivals rate λ, find the first departure probability.
similar_questions.solution: Memorylessness makes the residual service Exp(μ) at every service age. Racing independent exponentials gives p=μ/(λ+μ), and variance μλ/(λ+μ)².
